statement: A two-digit number is 4 times the sum of its digits. When 27 is added to it, the result is the number with the same two digits in the opposite order. What is the number?

choices.misconception: I found the digits 3 and 6 and gave their sum instead of the number.
I checked only the first condition, 12 = 4 x 3, and did not test adding 27.
I checked only the second condition, 25 + 27 = 52, and did not test the digit sum.
I found the right two digits but put the larger one in the tens place.

hints: Test each choice against both conditions.
With five candidates, checking each one against the conditions is faster than setting up equations. Discard any choice that fails either test; exactly one survives both.
Of the choices, only 12 and 36 are 4 times their digit sum. Add 27 to each and see which one reverses.

solutions.reliable: Check the choices. 9 is not a two-digit number. 12: digit sum 3 and 4 x 3 = 12 works, but 12 + 27 = 39, not 21. 25: 4 x 7 = 28, so it fails. 36: 4 x 9 = 36 works, and 36 + 27 = 63, its reverse. 63: 4 x 9 = 36, not 63, so it fails. The number is 36. The transferable idea: when the choices are candidate solutions, testing them against every condition can beat algebra.
solutions.elegant: With digits a and b, 10a + b = 4(a + b) gives b = 2a, and adding 27 to reverse the digits means b = a + 3. So a = 3 and b = 6, and the number is 36.

whyOnTest: Back-solving rewards checking every condition: two wrong choices pass one test each, so stopping at the first match is the trap.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
